why: An AI app is not finished on launch day. Models change and get retired, users write in new ways, data changes, and the bill grows without you noticing. Companies in Tunisia and in Europe want an AI engineer who can keep a feature working six months and a year after the demo: switch the model without breaking anything, improve it with numbers rather than gut feeling, and know what to do when something goes wrong. This is the last course of the track: the job that starts after the launch.
outcome: You plan a model and SDK migration safely (eval, canary, rollback), keep prompts in git with versions and audits, turn user feedback into eval cases, improve quality and cost with hill-climbing, handle an incident and write a post-mortem and a runbook, and build a portfolio that shows you can maintain an AI app.

lessons.title: Why does an AI app change on its own? Drift and maintenance
text: In a regular app, if you don't touch the code, the app keeps working exactly as it is. In an app with an LLM, it doesn't. On launch day the eval scores 93%, and six months later the support team complains that tickets now go to the wrong queue, even though nobody changed a single line. This is called drift: the app slowly moves away from the behaviour you want. This course teaches you how to catch it and how to improve the app over time.

Drift comes from three places. First: models change. A new model comes out, the old one becomes deprecated, and one day it is retired and returns 404. Example: claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022 was retired in October 2025. Even between generations, defaults change: on Claude Opus 5 the default effort is 'high', on Opus 5.5 it is 'medium'. If you didn't set effort explicitly, behaviour and cost change the day you switch the id.

Second: users change. You start with customers writing in French, then many start writing in Derja with Latin letters, or ask about things that weren't in the prompt (a new product, a Ramadan promotion). Your eval set keeps measuring the old world. Third: data changes: prices, the FAQ, the catalogue, the RAG documents, regulations. A prompt that says 'delivery costs 7 dinars' starts lying the day the price changes.

So maintenance in AI is not just 'we fix bugs'. It's a routine: monitor (we covered monitoring in the production course), read the provider's release notes, rerun the eval (covered in the evals course) after every change, collect feedback, and improve step by step. And the first condition: everything that can change (model id, effort, prompt version, eval set) is written in one place, in git, not scattered across ten files.

Think of it like a car: you don't wait for the engine to die before changing the oil. Set a calendar: feedback triage every week, migration notes and an eval run for every new model, a prompt audit every quarter. And everything has an owner and a backup, so that when someone goes on leave or changes jobs, the app isn't left orphaned.
points: Drift = the app changes without you changing the code: the model, the users, the data.
The model id is pinned (for example 'claude-opus-5-5' with no date) and changes only through a reviewed PR.
Set effort explicitly: the default differs from model to model.
Maintenance = a calendar + an owner + an eval, not a reaction when something breaks.

example.code:
# ai_config.yaml - everything that can drift lives in one reviewed file
app: support-tickets
model:
  id: claude-opus-5-5        # pinned id, changed only through a reviewed PR
  effort: medium             # set explicitly: the default differs between models
  max_tokens: 16000
prompt:
  file: prompts/ticket_system.md
  version: "2026-10-30.1"    # logged with every request
eval:
  set: evals/tickets_v4.jsonl  # anonymised real messages with the expected ticket
  min_accuracy: 0.92           # a release below this score is blocked
  last_run: "2026-11-02"
routine:
  feedback_triage: weekly
  migration_notes: every model release
  prompt_audit: every model release and every quarter
owners:
  primary: ines
  backup: karim
example.note: This format isn't a standard: it's an example. What matters is that the app reads the model and the prompt version from one reviewed file, and that every change to it goes through an eval.

lessons.title: Model migration: switch the model without breaking anything
text: Why switch models? Sometimes because the new one is better and cheaper: Claude Opus 5.5 costs $4 / $20 per million tokens instead of $5 / $25 for Opus 5, and does the same work with fewer tokens. And sometimes because the old one is about to be retired. But a migration is a production change like any other: the new model can refuse something the old one accepted, give longer answers, or return 400 on parameters that used to work.

Step one: read the provider's migration notes. Anthropic splits the changes in two: [BLOCKS] if you forget them, you get a 400 or a broken loop, and [TUNE] they affect quality or cost. Example Opus 5 -> Opus 5.5: thinking={'type': 'disabled'} and budget_tokens return 400 (thinking is always on, the control is effort); tool_choice 'any' or 'tool' returns 400 (use 'auto' + strict: true + say which tool in the prompt, and check that the call happened); the default effort became 'medium'; a safety classifier (bio) was added, so you must handle refusals; and switching models invalidates the cache (the first request writes it again).

Step two: the code goes in a branch, and you rerun the eval on both models with the same cases: score, cost per task, latency, refusal rate. Watch out for changes that raise no error: for example Haiku 4.5 -> Haiku 5.5, the same text becomes roughly 30% more tokens (new tokenizer). Rerun count_tokens on the new model, check max_tokens, and update the dashboards' baseline before anyone panics. Also, temperature and prefill return 400 on Haiku 5.5.

Step three: roll out gradually. Shadow: the new model gets a copy of the real traffic in the background, the user only sees the old model's answer, and you compare. Canary: 5% of requests really get the new model's answer, you watch the numbers, then 25%, 50%, 100%. In conversations, keep the same model from start to finish: the cache is per model, and one model's thinking blocks aren't always readable by another.

Step four: a rollback ready to go. The old model stays in the config until you're sure, and going back = flipping a flag (CANARY_SHARE = 0) with no redeploy. And log response.model: it tells you who really answered, not what you wrote in the config. Once the migration is done, run a prompt audit (lesson 4) and an effort sweep (lesson 6) on the new model: each in its own PR.
points: [BLOCKS] must be fixed before the deploy; [TUNE] are tested on the eval.
Change one thing at a time: the model first, prompt tuning later in its own PR.
Log response.model so you can compare the canary groups.
Shadow doubles the cost while it runs: set a duration and a budget up front.

example.code:
import random

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()

STABLE = {"model": "claude-opus-5", "effort": "high"}
CANDIDATE = {"model": "claude-opus-5-5", "effort": "medium"}  # set effort explicitly, then sweep it
CANARY_SHARE = 0.05  # 5% of requests; set it to 0.0 to roll back without a deploy


def pick_config():
    # Fine for one-shot requests; a conversation must stay on one model from start to end
    return CANDIDATE if random.random() < CANARY_SHARE else STABLE


def classify(message):
    cfg = pick_config()
    response = client.messages.create(
        model=cfg["model"],
        max_tokens=16000,  # thinking counts toward max_tokens
        output_config={"effort": cfg["effort"]},
        # Removed during the migration (both return 400 on claude-opus-5-5):
        #   thinking={"type": "disabled"}
        #   tool_choice={"type": "tool", "name": "..."}
        system="Classify the customer message: billing, network, sales or other. Answer with one word.",
        messages=[{"role": "user", "content": message}],
    )
    # Log which model really answered, to compare the two groups on the dashboard
    print("served_by", response.model, "stop", response.stop_reason,
          "out_tokens", response.usage.output_tokens)
    if response.stop_reason == "refusal":
        return None  # handle refusals before reading the content
    return "".join(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text").strip()
example.note: Picking at random per request works for classification. For a chatbot, pick the group per user or per conversation and keep it fixed.

lessons.title: The SDK and the API version: upgrades without surprises
text: Three things each have their own version: the model, the SDK (the 'anthropic' package you pip install), and the API version (the 'anthropic-version' header the SDK sends with every request). Each upgrade has its own breaking changes. Don't mix them in the same PR: if something breaks, you'll know the cause.

The SDK: pin the version in requirements.txt (for example 'anthropic>=1,<2') and in the lockfile, and upgrade on purpose, in a branch, after reading the SDK's changelog or MIGRATION.md. A real example: the Python SDK from 0.x to 1.x. It needs Python 3.10 or later. The HTTP layer became httpx2 (this only matters if you pass httpx objects to the SDK, for example a custom transport, and mocks like respx may no longer see the traffic). client.completions.create (the old Text Completions) was removed: you need messages.create. temperature, top_p and top_k are no longer accepted (TypeError). And output_format={...} as a dict becomes output_config={'format': {...}}; but output_format=Model with parse stays.

The API version is a date in the header. Anthropic ships API breaking changes in a new version, and your code moves when it's ready. Version '2026-10-21': temperature, top_p and top_k return 400 on all models, even with the default value; a 'document' block directly in an 'assistant' message returns 400; and a 'text' block with 'citations' in a 'user' message returns 400. And watch out: Python SDK 2.0.0 sends '2026-10-21' by default, so upgrading to 2.x also changes the API version. Batches you created before finish on the old version.

The method: an inventory with grep (temperature, completions.create, output_format, httpx), sort each hit (sometimes 'temperature' is a sensor variable: leave it alone), fix, run a type checker (pyright or mypy finds most call sites), run the tests, and finally one small real request (small max_tokens, because it's billed). If the production server is still on Python 3.9, that's a team decision: pip will keep installing the last 0.x without telling you anything.

So the backlog doesn't pile up: let a tool like Dependabot or Renovate open PRs for upgrades, but never auto-merge a major version. A small upgrade every month is far easier than a two-year jump in a single day, when the old model is retired and you're under pressure.
points: Model, SDK, API version: three different upgrades, each in its own PR.
pip index versions anthropic shows the published versions before you write the pin.
Pin the Python version in CI: on 3.9 pip silently stays on 0.x.
After the upgrade, a smoke test: response.model, stop_reason and output parsing.

example.code:
# requirements.txt - pin the major version and upgrade on purpose, in a branch:
#   anthropic>=1,<2
import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()
print("anthropic SDK", anthropic.__version__)

SCHEMA = {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {"category": {"type": "string", "enum": ["billing", "network", "sales", "other"]}},
    "required": ["category"],
    "additionalProperties": False,
}

# Before (SDK 0.x, older model):
# client.beta.messages.create(
#     model="claude-sonnet-4-6", max_tokens=1024, temperature=0.2,
#     output_format={"type": "json_schema", "schema": SCHEMA},
#     messages=[...],
# )

# After (SDK 1.x): no sampling parameters, the schema moves into output_config
response = client.messages.create(
    model="claude-sonnet-5-5",
    max_tokens=2048,
    output_config={"effort": "low", "format": {"type": "json_schema", "schema": SCHEMA}},
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "El facture mte3i ghalta, 5allast zouz marrat"}],
)

# Smoke test after the upgrade: the right model answered and the output is usable
assert response.model.startswith("claude-sonnet-5-5"), response.model
assert response.stop_reason == "end_turn", response.stop_reason
print(next(b.text for b in response.content if b.type == "text"))
example.note: The message in the example is written in Latin-letter Derja, the way customers write. The smoke test is billed: keep it small and don't run it on every commit.

lessons.title: Prompts in git: versioning, review and prompt audits
text: A prompt is code: it changes the product's behaviour as much as changing a function does. Yet many teams leave it as a string in the middle of a Python file, or in an admin panel anyone can edit in production. The result: nobody knows which prompt gave which answer, and bugs become impossible to explain.

The rules: each prompt in its own file (prompts/ticket_system.md) in git. Every change goes through a PR, reviewed by someone else, with the eval result in the PR description. Each version has an id (date + number) that is logged with every request (prompt_version, model, request_id): when a wrong answer comes in, you find the exact prompt. And a CHANGELOG says why it changed and what happened to the score. Rollback becomes easy: you go back to the previous version in the config.

The prompt audit: prompts pile up instructions written for older models. Current models follow instructions more literally, so the old crutches do harm. What to look for: pressure language ('CRITICAL', 'MUST', 'NEVER' in capitals, '!!!') that makes the model overdo it (over-triggering): say it normally, once, with the reason. Scaffolds that features have replaced: 'think step by step' or '<scratchpad>' become adaptive thinking + effort; 'answer only in JSON' + prefill + retry become structured outputs. Fossils: workarounds for a retired model, a 'reminder' repeated every turn, and limits like 'maximum 50 words' that choke the reasoning.

What to keep: the context only you know: the audience, the product, business rules with their reasons (refund ceiling, data rules), and the tools' contract. The question for each line: 'can the model know this on its own?' If not, keep it. And removing is a hypothesis, not a conclusion: remove a line or a block, rerun the eval, and if the score drops, bring it back in simpler wording. Before removing, grep for the full text: sometimes tests or log parsers compare against it.

Who reviews? A developer + someone from the business side (a support lead, for example) for the wording and the rules. In Tunisia teams are small, and sometimes you're on your own: even then, open a PR for yourself and let CI run the eval. And redo the prompt audit with every new model: prompts are per-model artefacts, and what one generation needs can be too much for the next.
points: Log prompt_version with every request: without it you can't explain any bug.
A prompt audit with every new model and every quarter.
Remove one thing at a time and measure; if the score drops, bring it back simpler.
The CHANGELOG says why, not just what changed.

example.code:
# prompts/CHANGELOG.md

## 2026-10-30.1 - ticket_system.md (PR #212, reviewed by Karim)
Why: prompt audit after the move to claude-opus-5-5.
- Removed: "CRITICAL: You MUST ALWAYS answer in valid JSON!!!"
  -> the JSON shape is enforced by output_config.format (structured outputs).
- Removed: "Think step by step before answering."
  -> thinking is always on; its depth is set with effort, not with prose.
- Rewritten: "NEVER invent an order id" -> "Use null when the message has no order id:
  agents search orders by this field, and a wrong id opens another customer's order."
- Kept: refunds above 50 TND go to a human (business rule, with its reason).
Eval (test split): accuracy 0.93 -> 0.94, cost per ticket -6%.

## 2026-09-12.2 - ticket_system.md (PR #188, reviewed by Ines)
Why: weekly triage found 14 Derja messages in Latin letters sent to 'other'.
- Added three varied examples in Latin-letter Derja, labelled as illustrative.
Eval (test split): accuracy 0.90 -> 0.93.
example.note: Each entry has the reason, the PR, the reviewer and the effect on the eval. The refund rule stays because it's a business rule, not a crutch for the model.

lessons.title: User feedback and logs: from a mistake to an eval case
text: The best eval cases come from production: real messages, real mistakes. The eval set you wrote on launch day measures what you imagined; production shows you what users really do. The job: catch the mistakes, understand them, and turn them into tests so they don't come back.

The sources: explicit feedback (thumbs up / thumbs down next to the answer, a 'report' button), and implicit feedback: a support agent corrects the category (the strongest signal, because it contains the right answer), the user asks the same question again, asks for a human, or leaves the conversation. And the logs: stop_reason 'refusal' or 'max_tokens', JSON that fails validation, lots of retries, high latency, a request with an odd cost. Log request_id, prompt_version, model and tokens; the user's full text only if you truly need it.

Weekly triage: take a sample: all the thumbs-down + 50 random conversations (most users say nothing when the answer is wrong). Read, and give each mistake a failure category: wrong category, invented order number, wrong language, refusal of a normal request, answer too long, outdated info (FAQ not updated). Count the mistakes in each category: the biggest one is your next piece of work. Keep the category list stable so you can compare week to week, and add a new category only if you really need it.

From a mistake to an eval case: anonymisation (in Tunisia, phone numbers and CIN numbers both have 8 digits, plus emails), the right answer from the human's correction, tags (failure type, language), and a source. Regex isn't perfect: have a human look at new cases before they go into the eval set. And new cases are split randomly between train and test (lesson 6), not all on one side.

Privacy: users' messages are personal data. Say in the privacy policy that feedback may be used to improve the service, keep raw data for as short a time as possible, and delete it after anonymisation. This is required by Tunisian personal data protection law, and by the GDPR if you have users in Europe. And an eval set with no personal data can be shared with the team and put in git without worry.
points: A human's correction = the best label: it contains the right answer.
Take a random sample too, not just the thumbs-down.
Stable failure categories let you compare week to week.
Don't put personal data in the eval set: it gets shared, committed and sent to the API.

example.code:
import json
import re

# Tunisian phone numbers and CIN numbers both have 8 digits: mask any 8-digit number
EIGHT_DIGITS = re.compile(r"(?<!\d)(?:\+216\s?)?\d{2}\s?\d{3}\s?\d{3}(?!\d)")
EMAIL = re.compile(r"[\w.+-]+@[\w-]+\.[\w.]+")


def anonymize(text):
    text = EMAIL.sub("<email>", text)
    return EIGHT_DIGITS.sub("<number>", text)


def feedback_to_cases(feedback_path, eval_path):
    """Turn answers corrected by the support team into new eval cases."""
    added = 0
    with open(feedback_path, encoding="utf-8") as src, \
            open(eval_path, "a", encoding="utf-8") as out:
        for line in src:
            fb = json.loads(line)
            # Keep only the cases where a human gave the right answer
            if fb["rating"] != "down" or not fb.get("corrected_category"):
                continue
            case = {
                "id": f"fb-{fb['request_id']}",
                "input": anonymize(fb["message"]),
                "expected": {"category": fb["corrected_category"]},
                "tags": [fb.get("failure_type", "untriaged"), fb["language"]],
                "source": "user_feedback",
            }
            out.write(json.dumps(case, ensure_ascii=False) + "\n")
            added += 1
    return added


print(feedback_to_cases("feedback_2026-11-03.jsonl", "evals/new_cases.jsonl"), "new cases to review")
example.note: The script writes to new_cases.jsonl, not straight into the eval set: a human reviews the anonymisation and the answer, then adds them.

lessons.title: The improvement loop: hill-climbing, cost and performance
text: Improving without an eval is change and hope. Hill-climbing: run the eval, read the failures, change one thing, rerun, keep it only if it's better and revert it if not, and repeat until the score stops rising or the budget runs out. The goal can be quality going up, or cost or latency going down with quality holding steady.

The split: train (you read its transcripts) and test (you never read it, you only measure it). The split is random, stratified by tags (language, category), and never based on the score. Why? When you read failures, you fix exactly those cases, and the score on them rises without the app really improving. The number you report is the test difference between the baseline and the final version. And generalise: describe the wrong behaviour, don't paste words from the train cases into the prompt.

Noise: for a pass rate, the margin (95%) is roughly 1/sqrt(n x reps): 25 test cases with 2 reps is about ±14 points, 50 with 2 about ±10. So +2 points on 25 cases is noise. Hence: changes big enough to show (a whole section, a new rule, not a word), more cases or reps, and plateau = 3 rounds with no gain. Each round: one change, run the full set, and record it in a table (round, the change, test, train, cost/task). And check response.model: the model you're counting must be the one that answered.

Cost: measure it per completed task, not per token: a cheap model that makes mistakes pays for the retry and for the human who fixes it. The levers, in order. The first ones don't lower quality: caching (it stays on all the time; check cache_read_input_tokens, as in the Claude API course), leaner input (prompt audit, large documents behind a tool), output (max_tokens is a safeguard, not a tuning knob; shorten answers with a clear format), and the Batches API for work nobody is waiting on (50%, and it stacks with caching). Then the tradeoffs: an effort sweep before you touch the model, and the model last. And before stepping down to a smaller model, check whether there's a newer model in the same tier at lower effort: sometimes it's the cheapest per task.

Each lever in its own diff: if it saved money and lowered accuracy, it's not an optimisation, revert it. Measure the tail too: the hardest 10% of cases are where the money goes and where the cheap model fails. And after every migration, redo the effort sweep from the new model's default; don't carry over the old level.
points: Train = read; test = measure. The score you report always comes from test.
One change per round, so you know what made the difference.
Caching, input, output, batch first; then effort; the model last.
max_tokens protects against an answer that never ends; it's not a way to cut cost.

example.code:
import json
import random

import anthropic

client = anthropic.Anthropic()
PRICES = {"claude-opus-5-5": (4.00, 20.00), "claude-sonnet-5-5": (2.00, 10.00)}  # USD per 1M tokens

with open("evals/tickets_v4.jsonl", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    cases = [json.loads(line) for line in f]

# Fixed seed: the same random split every round. You read train failures, you report test.
rng = random.Random(42)
rng.shuffle(cases)
cut = len(cases) // 2
train, test = cases[:cut], cases[cut:]


def run(cases, system, model, effort):
    passed, cost = 0, 0.0
    for case in cases:
        r = client.messages.create(
            model=model,
            max_tokens=4000,
            system=system,
            output_config={"effort": effort},
            messages=[{"role": "user", "content": case["input"]}],
        )
        if r.stop_reason == "end_turn":  # a refusal or a cut-off answer counts as a failure
            answer = "".join(b.text for b in r.content if b.type == "text").strip()
            passed += answer == case["expected"]["category"]
        p_in, p_out = PRICES[model]
        cost += (r.usage.input_tokens * p_in + r.usage.output_tokens * p_out) / 1_000_000
    return passed / len(cases), cost / len(cases)


with open("prompts/ticket_system.md", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    SYSTEM = f.read()

# One change per round: here only effort moves, the prompt and the model stay frozen
for effort in ["medium", "low"]:
    acc_train, _ = run(train, SYSTEM, "claude-opus-5-5", effort)
    acc_test, cost = run(test, SYSTEM, "claude-opus-5-5", effort)
    print(f"{effort}: train={acc_train:.2f} test={acc_test:.2f} cost/task=${cost:.5f}")
example.note: The cost here leaves out caching to keep the code short. Every run is billed: work out the budget first (number of cases x configs x cost per task) and use the Batches API for big sweeps.

lessons.title: Incidents, post-mortems and documentation
text: An incident in an AI feature sometimes has no 500 error at all: everything returns 200, but the answers are wrong. The kinds: bad outputs (more hallucinations, wrong language, every ticket going to 'other'), outage or overload (5xx, 529, timeouts), more refusals after a model change, a sudden cost spike (a loop that doesn't stop, a broken cache), and security (prompt injection, covered in the production course).

To detect them: alerts on quality signals, not just on errors: the category distribution, refusal rate, rate of JSON that fails validation, thumbs-down rate, cost per hour, p95 latency. And very often someone in support notices before the dashboard does: give them a clear channel to report it.

When it happens: mitigate first, understand later. The levers must be ready before the incident: a rollback of the prompt or the model with a config flag; a kill switch that turns the feature off and serves a fallback (an 'an agent will reply to you' message, or a queue to a human); and for outages, retries and a second model if you planned one. Communicate: tell the support team what's going on. Then repair the data (for example, re-classify the wrong tickets with a batch).

The blameless post-mortem: timeline, impact, root cause, what went well and what didn't, and actions, each with an owner and a date. You don't look for who made the mistake: you look for the gap in the process. In AI, the most important action: the incident becomes eval cases and an alert, so the same mistake can't slip through a PR again.

Documentation and handover: a RUNBOOK.md with the architecture, where the prompts live, the model ids and why they were chosen, how to run the eval, the dashboards and alerts, how to roll back, the names of the secrets (never the values), cost and limits, and the owners. Plus a decisions log ('why Sonnet and not Opus for tickets', with the eval numbers). At handover, the new person does a practice rollback with their own hands. And if you freelance, delivering a runbook with the project makes the client trust you and come back.
points: Mitigate before the root cause: roll back to the version that works, then understand.
A rollback you've never tested isn't a rollback: test it once a quarter.
Every incident leaves eval cases and an alert behind.
The runbook has the names of the secrets, never their values.

example.code:
# Post-mortem: wrong ticket categories after a prompt change (2026-10-14)

Severity: medium - no data leak, about 900 tickets sent to the wrong queue
Duration: 09:40 -> 11:05 (85 minutes)

## Timeline
- 09:10 Prompt 2026-10-14.1 deployed (PR #201: "shorter system prompt")
- 09:40 Support lead: "everything goes to 'other'"; dashboard: 'other' 6% -> 41%
- 09:52 Rollback: PROMPT_VERSION=2026-10-02.3 (config flag, no redeploy)
- 10:05 'other' back to 7%; misrouted tickets re-classified with a batch job
- 11:05 Incident closed

## Root cause
The PR removed the definitions of the categories, judged "too long".
The eval still passed: tickets_v3 had only 4 'payment' cases.

## What went well / what went badly
- Rollback in 12 minutes thanks to the version flag.
- No alert on the category distribution: a human noticed first.

## Actions (owner, date)
- [ ] Add 40 anonymised 'payment' cases to the eval (Ines, 2026-10-21)
- [ ] Alert when one category moves more than 15 points in an hour (Karim, 2026-10-24)
- [ ] Prompt PRs show the eval score per category, not only the total (Ines, 2026-10-28)
example.note: No person's name in the root cause: the problem was an eval with only 4 'payment' cases and no alert.

lessons.title: Your path as an AI engineer: portfolio, keeping up and lifelong learning
text: You've reached the end of the track: from tokens and your first call, to prompts, the API, agents, RAG, evals, production, and now maintenance. The difference between a junior who gets hired and one who doesn't isn't the number of demos: it's showing that you can measure, maintain and improve. Recruiters in Tunisia and in Europe ask 'how do you know it works?' and 'what do you do when the model changes?'. Now you have an answer.

The portfolio: 2 or 3 complete projects, each with an eval set and numbers, cost per task, a CHANGELOG showing the iterations (v1 -> v4), a README with the limits, and a 'how it is maintained' section. A small project you worked on for months (you switched the model, added cases from feedback, cut the cost) is worth more than 10 demos. And multilingual Derja/French/Arabic is a real strength: European companies rarely have that data and that understanding.

Keeping up: AI changes every month. The primary sources: the official documentation, the providers' release notes and migration guides (Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, Mistral...), and the SDKs' changelogs. The method: when a new model comes out, run your eval on your own projects before you believe the benchmarks and the hype. Half an hour of reading a week and one experiment a month are enough to stay up to date. And watch out for old tutorials: temperature and prefill no longer work on the new models.

Paths: AI engineer in a product team, LLMOps or platform, freelance (automation, integrations, chatbots), consulting for Tunisian SMEs, or remote with a European company. Deepen the foundations: Python and software engineering (tests, CI), SQL, cloud, evaluation, security. And the soft skills: explain limits to the client, write clearly, estimate cost before you start. In interviews, have a story ready about a real mistake and how you measured and fixed it: it convinces far more than 'everything went well'.

Learning never ends. Share what you learn: an article in Derja, French or English, a short meetup talk, an open source contribution (documentation, a small fix), and help the juniors who come after you: explaining something to someone else is the best way to understand it. A 90-day plan: month one, a project + an eval; month two, deploy + logs + a feedback loop; month three, a migration or a cost optimisation documented in the CHANGELOG + an article. Congratulations on finishing the track, and now get started.

example.code:
# derja-ticket-router

Routes customer messages (Tunisian Derja in Arabic or Latin letters, French, Arabic)
to the right support queue with the Claude API.

## Results (eval: 200 anonymised messages, scores on the 100-case test split)
| Version | Model / effort | Accuracy | Cost per 1000 messages |
|---|---|---|---|
| v1 | claude-opus-5-5 / medium | 0.88 | $2.10 |
| v3 | claude-opus-5-5 / medium + Derja examples | 0.94 | $2.30 |
| v4 | claude-haiku-5-5 / low | 0.93 | $0.09 |

## How it is maintained
- Model id, effort and prompt version live in config.yaml; every change is a PR with an eval run
- Every week, answers flagged by users become new eval cases (personal data masked)
- CHANGELOG.md lists every prompt change and its effect on the score

## Limits
- Messages mixing Derja and French slang are still the weakest group (0.86)
- No message text is stored: logs keep request ids, versions and token counts

## Run it
pip install -r requirements.txt, set ANTHROPIC_API_KEY in the environment, then: python -m router.eval

exercises.q: You have code running on claude-opus-5 with: thinking={'type': 'disabled'}, tool_choice={'type': 'tool', 'name': 'create_ticket'}, no effort, and a system prompt containing 'CRITICAL: you MUST use the tool'. You're moving it to claude-opus-5-5. Classify each item as [BLOCKS] or [TUNE] and say what you do.
exercises.hint: What returns 400 on Opus 5.5, and what only changes quality or cost?
exercises.answer: [BLOCKS] The model id -> 'claude-opus-5-5'. [BLOCKS] thinking disabled returns 400: remove it; the control becomes output_config.effort (start with 'low' if latency matters, and measure). [BLOCKS] tool_choice 'tool' returns 400: 'auto' + 'strict': True on the tool + 'Use the create_ticket tool' in the prompt, and check in code that there is a tool_use, retrying if not. [BLOCKS] handle stop_reason 'refusal' before reading the content. [TUNE] set effort explicitly (the default became 'medium' instead of 'high') and run a sweep. [TUNE] 'CRITICAL: you MUST' becomes 'Use the create_ticket tool when...': new models follow instructions literally. [TUNE] check max_tokens (thinking counts toward it) and the rate limits of the new pool.

exercises.q: Write a function served_by(response, expected, newer=()) that returns True if the expected model is the one that answered, without confusing 'claude-opus-5' and 'claude-opus-5-5'.
exercises.answer:
def served_by(response, expected, newer=()):
    """True when the expected model answered.

    response.model is checked with startswith, so list the longer ids that share
    the prefix: "claude-opus-5-5" also starts with "claude-opus-5".
    """
    model = response.model
    return model.startswith(expected) and not any(model.startswith(n) for n in newer)


# Usage during a canary on claude-opus-5 -> claude-opus-5-5:
# served_by(r, "claude-opus-5", newer=["claude-opus-5-5"])   # stable group
# served_by(r, "claude-opus-5-5")                            # candidate group

exercises.q: This week's triage has 40 thumbs-down. 18 are a wrong category on Latin-letter Derja messages, 9 an invented order number, 7 an outdated FAQ (the delivery price changed), and 6 the user was just annoyed and the answer was right. What do you do, in order?
exercises.hint: Not everything gets fixed in the prompt, and not every mistake is the model's.
exercises.answer: 1) The 7 FAQ ones: this is data, not the model: fix the FAQ (and add a check on its last-update date), no eval round needed. 2) The 18 (the biggest category): anonymise, add the cases to the eval with the right answer, split them randomly between train and test, then one improvement round (for example varied examples in Latin-letter Derja) and measure on test. 3) The 9: eval cases + a clear rule 'null if there is no number' with the reason, or a check in code that the number exists in the database. 4) The 6: change nothing in the model; record them as 'not a model failure'. And add 50 random conversations to next week's triage, so you don't only see the people who complain.

exercises.q: Write a function should_rollback(stable, canary) that returns a list of reasons if the canary must stop: accuracy dropped by more than 2 points, refusals above max(1%, twice the stable rate), or cost per task more than 1.5 times higher.
A colleague tells you: 'I read all 60 cases, fixed the prompt 12 times, and the score went from 0.86 to 0.95 on those same 60.' Why don't you trust that number, and what do you suggest?
exercises.answer: Because they read the cases they measure on: the changes fixed exactly those 60 (overfitting), and we don't know whether the app improved on new messages. Also, 12 changes together don't tell you which one made the difference, and on 60 cases the margin is about ±13 points (1/sqrt(60)). The suggestion: a random split (stratified by tags) into train and test, read only train, one change per round, rerun the full set, and the number reported is the test difference between the baseline and the final version. And if needed, add cases or reps.

exercises.q: After a migration from Haiku 4.5 to Haiku 5.5, the dashboard shows +30% tokens and some truncated answers. The manager is worried. Explain what's happening and say what you do.
exercises.hint: Think about the tokenizer and thinking.
exercises.answer: Haiku 5.5 has a new tokenizer: the same text becomes roughly 30% more tokens, so usage goes up even if the work is the same. But Haiku 5.5's per-token price ($0.10 / $0.50 when the prompt is 100K or less) is much lower than Haiku 4.5's ($1 / $5), so we have to compare cost per task in dollars, not tokens. The truncated answers: thinking is now on by default and counts toward max_tokens, and max_tokens was sized for the old tokenizer: we raise it and watch for stop_reason 'max_tokens'. We rerun count_tokens on claude-haiku-5-5, try effort 'low' on the eval, and update the dashboards' baseline.

exercises.q: You're leaving, and handing an AI project over to a new developer. List what must be in the RUNBOOK.md (at least 7 items).
exercises.answer: 1) The architecture: who calls the API, from where, and what the flows are. 2) The model ids and effort, and why we chose them (decisions log with eval numbers). 3) Where the prompts live, how versions change, and the CHANGELOG. 4) How to run the eval (command, the set, the threshold). 5) The dashboards and alerts, and what normal values look like. 6) Rollback and the kill switch: the flags and commands, with the last time they were tested. 7) The names of the secrets and where they're set (never the values). 8) Cost: how much per month, the limits and the budget alerts. 9) The routine: weekly triage, migration notes, prompt audit. 10) The owners and how to communicate during an incident. And to finish: a handover session where the new person does a practice rollback with their own hands.

pitfalls: The model id written in ten places in the code, and effort left at the default: on migration day you forget one place, and behaviour changes without you knowing why.
Changing the model, the prompt and the SDK in the same PR: when something breaks you don't know the cause, and the rollback also reverts the good changes.
Improving the prompt while reading the cases you measure on, or deciding on a 2-point difference over 25 cases: that's overfitting and noise, not improvement.
Adding 'CRITICAL: MUST' for every bug and never removing anything: the prompt becomes a maze of special cases, and the new model overdoes it.
Putting raw user messages (CIN, phone numbers, emails) in the eval set and in git: the eval gets shared and sent to the API.
A rollback you never tested and no kill switch: on incident day you write code under pressure instead of flipping a flag.

Comparing models on price per token and stepping down to a smaller model before trying caching and effort: cost per completed task is what matters, and a model that makes mistakes pays for the retry and the human.

interview.q: Why does an app with an LLM change even if we didn't change the code?
interview.a: Because of drift, which comes from three places: models (new versions, deprecations, retirements, changing defaults such as effort), users (new languages and new questions), and data (FAQ, prices, documents). We detect it with monitoring on quality signals, weekly feedback triage, and an eval we rerun after every change. And we pin everything that can change in one config file in git.

interview.q: How do you migrate to a new model in production?
interview.a: I read the migration notes and separate [BLOCKS] (400s or loops) from [TUNE] (quality and cost). I fix the BLOCKS in a branch and run the eval on both models: score, cost per task, latency, refusals. Then shadow or a gradual canary, I log response.model, and rollback is a flag. Once it's stable, a prompt audit and an effort sweep on the new model, each in its own PR.

Each prompt is a file in git, every change is a PR with a review and the eval result, a version id is logged with every request (along with the model and the request_id), and a CHANGELOG records the why and the effect. Rollback = going back to the previous version in the config. And a prompt audit with every new model to remove instructions that are no longer needed.

interview.q: How do you turn user feedback into real improvement?
interview.a: We collect explicit feedback (thumbs) and implicit feedback (support corrections, escalations), plus signals from the logs (refusals, max_tokens, JSON that fails validation). Every week, triage on the thumbs-down and a random sample, classified with stable failure categories. The biggest category becomes anonymised eval cases with the right answer, then an improvement round measured on the test split.

interview.q: Why do a train / test split when you improve a prompt?
interview.a: Because when we read the failures we fix exactly those cases, and the score on them lies. We read train and only measure test, with a random, stratified split, never based on the score. The number we report is the difference on test. And we account for noise: roughly 1/sqrt(n x reps), so we don't believe a small difference.

interview.q: The API bill went up 40% this month. What do you do?
interview.a: Measure first: usage per traffic class (chat, overnight batch...). I check whether cache_read_input_tokens dropped (something dynamic got into the prefix, the model changed), whether there was a migration (tokenizer, default effort), a loop that doesn't stop, max_tokens, or more traffic. Then the levers in order: caching, input, output, batch, then effort, and the model last, each in its own diff with an eval, and we measure cost per completed task.

interview.q: Tell me about an incident in an AI feature and how you handled it.
interview.a: I tell it with a clear structure: what happened (for example every ticket going to 'other' after a new prompt), how it was detected, the mitigation (rollback with the flag in 12 minutes), the repair (re-classification with a batch), and the blameless post-mortem: the root cause (an eval with only 4 'payment' cases) and the actions: new eval cases, an alert on the distribution, a per-category score in PRs.

interview.q: How do you stay up to date in AI?
interview.a: The official documentation, the providers' release notes and migration guides, and the SDKs' changelogs. When a new model comes out, I run my eval on it before I believe the benchmarks. And I learn by doing and sharing: a small project a month, an article, a meetup.
